rationale: B wins because it keeps the caveat in the lede: "Peloton posts its first profitable quarter in three years — on adjusted EBITDA, not net income" is the honest story, not the confetti version. A has good machinery, but "Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash, Peloton Has More Loyal Subscribers Than Ever" imports a culture-story premise the update did not supply and turns a churn datapoint into a comeback mood board. B still has one swollen claim, "the hardware company is becoming a subscription company," but its refusals show the better editor was awake.
gaps_in_A: "Three Years After Its Pandemic Crash, Peloton Has More Loyal Subscribers Than Ever" imports the pandemic-crash frame; the update gives churn, members, adjusted EBITDA, debt, not a supplied culture-story premise.
"The prevailing belief is Peloton is in secular decline" is treated as fact before proof. That belongs in required evidence, not in the angle itself.
"Peloton Is Now Renting Bikes. The Target Customer Is Not Who Bought One in 2020" assumes a changed customer without rental price, uptake, or customer interviews.
Angles 4 and 5 both lean on "record-low churn" and "6 million"; different beat labels do not fully hide the same core story.
gaps_in_B: "the hardware company is becoming a subscription company" overstates the update; the facts support rental expansion, not a full company identity change.
"built itself on a $1,000+ hardware sale" is not in the supplied update. It may be true, but this exercise did not give it to you.
"Decay: 4hr" is over-precise theater. Same-day earnings urgency is real, but pretending the window is four hours adds fake rigor.
"churn is the number that decides whether a connected-fitness company survives" is a useful instinct, but it needs industry context before it becomes a claim.
